APPLICABLE LAW
General Principles of Property Valuation for Taxation Purposes. Under Washington
law, all property must be valued at “one hundred percent of . . . true and fair value.”7 True and
fair value is synonymous with fair market value,8 which “is the amount of money a buyer of
property willing but not obligated to buy would pay a seller of property willing but not obligated
to sell.”9 To reach an opinion of fair market value, the appraiser must consider a property’s
highest and best use,10 unless the use is prohibited “under existing zoning or land use planning
ordinances or statutes or other government restrictions.”11 In the course of determining a
property’s value, assessors must allocate the value to the land and the structures, giving care that
the sum of those values does not “exceed the true and fair value of the total property as it
exists.”12
Washington law13 requires that fair market value be determined using the sales
comparison approach, with further consideration of the cost and income capitalization
approaches if there are not sufficient comparable sales available. In the absence of a sufficient
number of comparable sales, or when valuing a complex property, either the cost or income
capitalization approach, or both, “must be the dominant factors in valuation.”14 The assessed
values of other properties do not constitute relevant evidence of the subject property’s market value,
nor does the assessed value of the subject property from a previous or subsequent assessment year.15
A comparison of assessed values is not a recognized appraisal practice, nor is it authorized by RCW
84.40.030(3).

property’s fair market value by considering sales of the property being appraised or sales of

ANALYSIS
For the Owners to prevail in this appeal, the hearing record must contain clear, cogent,
and convincing evidence that a value correction is in order. The evidence before the Board does
not meet this standard. Thus, the Board concludes the Owners have not met the burden of showing
it is highly probable the Assessor overvalued the subject property for assessment-year 2018.
Property tax valuation is governed by the applicable statutes. RCW 84.40.030(3) lists the
ways to value property, and the use of comparable sales is the preferred method listed. The
Assessor provides seven sales for consideration and compares the subject’s estimated completed
value to those sales. That estimated completion value of the subject falls within the range of the
Assessor’s sales.
The Owners argue that their objection is to the way the Assessor valued the land, and that
when looking at the assessed valuations of their neighbors, their assessed value is too high. The use
of assessed values, however, is not a statutorily approved method of valuation of property, nor is it a
component of any of the valuation methodologies recognized and used in accepted appraisal
practice.25
In University Village Ltd. Partners v. King County, University Village argued that because
its land was valued at a higher per-square-foot rate than its neighbors, that its assessment was a
violation of the uniformity clause, and that its land should be valued at the same per-square-foot rate
as its neighbors.26 In that case, the Assessor had valued the property using an income approach, and
then assigned a portion of that value each to the land and the improvements. The court explained
that taxes are assessed on the value of property as a whole (both land and improvements). To be
successful in challenging the land valuation, University Village would have had to show that the
value of the whole property was assessed in such a way that its assessment ratio was incorrect in
relation to similar properties. Although the issue in this case is not precisely the same, the Owners
are singling out the assessed value of the land, arguing that their property is overvalued in
comparison to other properties in their area. But the bulk of the data provided by the Owners looks
only at the assessed value of the land of these properties, not the overall value of the properties.
In Matalone v. Hara, BTA Docket No. 71193 (2010), copy attached, the Board spent
considerable time discussing why assessed values are not the same as sales prices and do not always

represent 100 percent of true and fair value because they are computed using mass appraisal models.
As explained in Matalone, “the appeal focus is on whether the Assessor’s methodology produced a
reasonable value for the property under review.”27
In this case, the Assessor provides comparable sales to support his value of the property that
was determined using his mass appraisal model.28 The methodology used by the Assessor to value
properties is explained in the Area Reports cited in footnote 24.
The Board gives no weight to the letter offer from the developer that the Owners submitted.
It appears to be an unsolicited inquiry, and not a negotiated price.
The Owners do not provide any market information to support their assertion of a lower
property value. While the Board understands their comparison to the assessed values of
neighboring properties, assessed values are simply not a statutorily allowed method to value
property.
DECISION
In accordance with RCW 84.08.130, the Board sustains the determination of the King
County Board of Equalization and orders the value as shown on page one of this decision. The
King County Assessor is hereby directed that the assessment and tax rolls of King County are to
accord with, and give full effect to, the provisions of this decision.

Right of Review
Pursuant to WAC 456-10-730, you may file a written exception to this Proposed
Decision. You must file the letter of exception with the Board of Tax Appeals
within 20 calendar days of the date the Proposed Decision is issued, by electronic
or U.S. mail. You also must serve a copy on all other parties. The written
exception must clearly specify the factual and legal grounds upon which the
exception is based. No new evidence may be introduced in the written exception,
nor may a party or parties raise an argument that was not raised at the hearing.
The other parties may submit a reply to the exception within 10 business
days. The Board will then consider the matter and issue a Final Decision. There
is no reconsideration from the Board’s Final Decision.
If no written exception is filed, the Proposed Decision becomes the Board’s Final
Decision 20 calendar days after issuance of the Proposed Decision.
